summaries.example: Imagine a school library. Many books contain different facts, but you might ask whether there is one basic idea that helps the books fit into an ordered collection. Petrizi’s philosophy asks a much larger question: is there one first source that helps explain everything else? He called this first source the One, and connected it with the Good.
summaries.summary: Joane Petrizi was a medieval Georgian philosopher especially interested in Platonism and Neoplatonism, a tradition that explains reality through a highest source and the levels that come from it. He translated Nemesius of Emesa’s work about human nature into Georgian. Most importantly, he translated Proclus’s Elementatio theologica and wrote a chapter-by-chapter commentary. Petrizi explained Proclus’s claim that the One is the origin of all the many things in the universe. He also connected the One with the Good, saying that other beings have goodness by sharing in it. Petrizi examined causes, knowledge, reason, and the movement from the One to many things and back toward the One. His work became important in Georgian culture and influenced Armenian and later Georgian readers. Scholars only began studying his writings in a thorough way much later.
key_ideas: Petrizi was a major medieval Georgian thinker, but very little reliable information about his life survives.
He translated a work by Proclus into Georgian and wrote a detailed explanation of it.
He believed that the One is the first source of being and that the One is also the Good.
He studied how causes produce other things and how human reason helps make knowledge possible.
His writings influenced Georgian thought and later helped spread Proclus’s philosophy beyond Georgia.
summaries.why_it_matters: Petrizi shows that philosophy was developed in many languages and places, not only in the most familiar parts of Europe. His translations and explanations helped old Greek ideas travel into Georgian and Armenian intellectual life. His work also reminds us that a careful commentator can add new arguments and examples instead of merely repeating an earlier author. Because information about his life is limited, his books are especially important for understanding his thought.

important_terms.definition: A Georgian philosopher from the medieval period who translated and explained important Greek philosophical works.
The idea of a first and highest unity that is the source of everything else.
The highest good, which Petrizi connected with the One and toward which all things are directed.
The process by which something receives a feature or value by sharing in a higher source.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher look for one first source behind many different things?
Can something be good because it shares in a greater good?
Why are translations and explanations important for keeping old ideas alive?

summaries.example: Consider a chain of explanations: a statue may be made from bronze, shaped by an artist, designed for a purpose, and produced through an action. Petrizi thought the usual Aristotelian list of four causes did not fully capture the kind of originating power emphasized in Proclus. He therefore added a creative cause. This illustrates his larger effort to reorganize causal explanation within a Neoplatonic picture in which reality proceeds from the One and ultimately turns back toward its source.
summaries.summary: Joane Petrizi was a major medieval Georgian interpreter of Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy. His biography is poorly documented, and scholars have revised their estimates of when he lived; the entry presents him as a twelfth-century thinker. Petrizi translated Nemesius of Emesa’s On the Nature of Man and translated Proclus’s Elementatio theologica into Georgian. His extensive commentary explains each proposition while developing Petrizi’s own philosophical project. At its center is the One, which he treats as the first principle of multiplicity, beyond ordinary being, and identical with the Good. Beings are good through participation in this higher source, and caused things are understood in relation to their cause and their return toward it. Petrizi also expands Proclus’s treatment of causality and argues that the traditional four Aristotelian causes need a fifth, creative cause. His epistemology gives reason a productive role in establishing knowledge and being. Later Georgian and Armenian thinkers used, adapted, or criticized his work, while modern scholarship eventually produced editions and studies of it.
key_ideas: Petrizi’s dates and biography remain uncertain, although current research characterizes him as a twelfth-century thinker.
His commentary interprets Proclus from within Proclus’s own philosophical system rather than treating the text only through outside assumptions.
The One is presented as the origin of multiplicity, while also being beyond ordinary beings and identical with the Good.
Petrizi describes reality through a movement from the One to the many and a return of caused things toward their cause.
He criticizes the adequacy of the Aristotelian causal framework for his purposes and adds a creative cause.
His account of reason and knowledge presents human thought as productive and as involved in establishing being.
summaries.why_it_matters: Petrizi matters both as a philosopher and as a transmitter of philosophy. He demonstrates how ancient Greek ideas were translated, interpreted, and transformed in medieval Georgia. His commentary is not simply a passive summary: it develops issues such as causality, the One, the Good, and the powers of reason. His later reception also shows that intellectual traditions can travel through multiple languages, with each translation opening possibilities for preservation, criticism, and reinterpretation.

important_terms.definition: A late ancient philosophical tradition associated with Plato that explains reality as ordered from a highest principle through levels of derivation and return.
Petrizi’s name for the first principle: a unity beyond ordinary beings and the source of the many.
The study of being and reality; for Petrizi, it includes the question of how beings depend on a first principle.
The study of knowledge. Petrizi emphasized reason’s active role in establishing being and making knowledge possible.
A relation in which a caused thing receives goodness or other features from a higher source without becoming identical with that source.
An account of what explains something. Petrizi accepted material, formal, efficient, and final causes and proposed a further creative cause.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining many things require a first principle, or could explanation continue without an origin?
What is gained or lost by adding a creative cause to a standard list of causes?
How does interpreting a philosopher from within that philosopher’s system differ from criticizing the system from outside?
If beings participate in the Good, does that make goodness independent of individual things or dependent on them?
Why might a translation change the history of philosophy even when the original ideas already exist?

summaries.example: Suppose you see many different trees in a park. You can describe each tree, but you might also ask what makes the whole park part of an ordered natural world. Petrizi’s answer begins with the idea of a first source, the One. The many things in the universe depend on it, just as branches depend on a tree’s deeper structure. The comparison is only an illustration: Petrizi’s One is not an ordinary object inside the universe.
summaries.summary: Joane Petrizi was one of the most important medieval Georgian philosophers. Reliable details about his life are scarce, so scholars have debated his dates, but his work is generally understood as belonging to the twelfth century. He translated Nemesius of Emesa’s discussion of human nature into Georgian and translated Proclus’s Elementatio theologica, adding a long commentary. Petrizi valued Plato and the Neoplatonic tradition, which explains reality as ordered from a highest source. In his reading of Proclus, the One is the origin of all multiplicity and is beyond ordinary beings. Petrizi identifies this One with the Good. Other things are good through participation in it, and all caused things ultimately turn back toward their cause. He also examines the relation between causes and effects, criticizing the limits of the Aristotelian account for his purposes and introducing a creative cause alongside material, formal, efficient, and final causes. His account of reason gives human thinking an active role in knowledge. Petrizi’s writings later shaped Georgian and Armenian discussions and became the subject of more systematic scholarship in the twentieth century.
key_ideas: We know little securely about Petrizi’s life, but his writings place him within medieval Georgian philosophy and show strong knowledge of ancient thinkers.
He translated Proclus’s Elementatio theologica and wrote a detailed commentary intended to make its difficult arguments more understandable.
Petrizi says the One is the source of the many and is not simply one being among other beings.
He connects the One with the Good: things become good by participating in the higher Good.
He describes a pattern of descent from the One into multiplicity and ascent from multiplicity back toward its cause.
He thought older accounts of causes were incomplete for his project and proposed a creative cause in addition to four familiar kinds.
summaries.why_it_matters: Petrizi’s story shows how philosophy moves across cultures. Greek works reached Georgian readers through translation, and Petrizi’s explanations helped them become part of Georgian intellectual life. His ideas were later reused and debated by Armenian and Georgian thinkers. Studying him also broadens the history of philosophy: important arguments about reality, causes, and knowledge were developed in medieval Georgia as well as in better-known philosophical centers.

important_terms.definition: A medieval Georgian philosopher known especially for translating and commenting on ancient Greek philosophy.
A philosophical tradition based on Plato that describes reality as flowing from a highest principle and returning toward it.
The first unity and source of all the many things that exist in Petrizi’s interpretation of Proclus.
The highest and purest good, which Petrizi identifies with the One.
The relation by which lower things receive goodness or other features from a higher source.
The study of how one thing explains or produces another. Petrizi distinguishes several kinds of causes and adds a creative one.

questions_to_think_about: Why would Petrizi say that the first principle cannot be just another being?
How might a commentator make a difficult book useful to a wider audience?
Do you think adding a new kind of cause changes how we explain events?
What could it mean for knowledge to depend on a first principle?
How can a philosophical text influence people who read it in a different language?
